Keywords: async def await non-blocking I/O concurrent database HTTP
Description: Define route handlers with async def and await all I/O. FastAPI runs sync def handlers in a threadpool automatically — but async def is required to properly await async DB drivers or async HTTP clients.
When to Use: Whenever the handler does any I/O: DB queries HTTP calls Redis file operations
Code Example:
"from fastapi import FastAPI

app = FastAPI()

@app.get('/items/{item_id}')
async def read_item(item_id: int):
    # all awaited I/O runs without blocking the event loop
    item = await db.get(Item, item_id)
    return item

# sync def is OK for CPU work or sync libraries:
@app.get('/compute')
def compute(x: float):
    return {'result': x * 42}"
Trade-offs: If you have a sync dependency (like psycopg2) wrap it in run_in_executor. Never call blocking I/O directly in async def — it blocks the entire event loop.

Keywords: BackgroundTasks add_task fire forget post-response email webhook non-blocking
Description: Use FastAPI's BackgroundTasks to run post-response work without delaying the response. Background tasks run after the response is sent in the same process.
When to Use: When work must happen after the response but doesn't affect what you return
Code Example:
"from fastapi import BackgroundTasks

def write_notification(email: str, message: str = ''):
    with open('log.txt', mode='a') as log:
        log.write(f'notification sent to {email}: {message}')

@app.post('/send-notification/{email}')
async def send_notification(email: str, background_tasks: BackgroundTasks):
    background_tasks.add_task(write_notification, email, message='some notification')
    return {'message': 'Notification sent in the background'}"
Trade-offs: Background tasks run in the same process — use Celery or ARQ for long tasks heavy fan-out or distributed execution.
Packages: none (built-in), celery or arq for heavy jobs

Keywords: StreamingResponse generator large file CSV download stream memory efficient
Description: Return StreamingResponse with an async or sync generator to stream large responses without loading everything into memory.
When to Use: When response bodies are too large to buffer (CSV exports video files large JSON arrays)
Code Example:
"from fastapi.responses import StreamingResponse
import csv, io

@router.get('/export')
async def export_csv():
    async def generate():
        output = io.StringIO()
        writer = csv.writer(output)
        writer.writerow(['id', 'email'])
        yield output.getvalue()
        output.seek(0)
        output.truncate()
        async for user in stream_users_from_db():
            writer.writerow([user.id, user.email])
            yield output.getvalue()
            output.seek(0)
            output.truncate()
    return StreamingResponse(generate(), media_type='text/csv',
                             headers={'Content-Disposition': 'attachment; filename=export.csv'})"
Trade-offs: Very memory efficient — no full dataset in RAM. Does not buffer so you cannot set Content-Length header.

Keywords: JSONResponse HTMLResponse PlainTextResponse ORJSONResponse UJSONResponse FileResponse media_type
Description: Return specific response class instances for non-JSON content or to use faster JSON serialisers. ORJSONResponse uses orjson for significantly faster JSON serialisation.
When to Use: When you need HTML text binary or faster JSON responses — or need full control over headers/status
Code Example:
"from fastapi.responses import ORJSONResponse, HTMLResponse, FileResponse

# Faster JSON with orjson:
@app.get('/items', response_class=ORJSONResponse)
async def list_items():
    return [{'id': 1}]

# HTML response:
@app.get('/page', response_class=HTMLResponse)
async def page():
    return '<html><body>Hello</body></html>'

# File download:
@app.get('/download')
async def download():
    return FileResponse('report.pdf', media_type='application/pdf')"
Trade-offs: orjson does not support all Python types that the standard json module does — check for datetime UUID Decimal support.

Keywords: connection pool AsyncEngine create_async_engine pool_size max_overflow pool_pre_ping SQLAlchemy
Description: Configure SQLAlchemy's create_async_engine with a connection pool. Reuse connections across requests instead of opening new ones per request.
When to Use: Always — essential for any production database-backed FastAPI app with async SQLAlchemy
Code Example:
"from sqlalchemy.ext.asyncio import create_async_engine, AsyncSession, async_sessionmaker

engine = create_async_engine(
    DATABASE_URL,
    pool_size=10,
    max_overflow=20,
    pool_pre_ping=True,  # auto-detects stale connections
)

AsyncSessionLocal = async_sessionmaker(engine, expire_on_commit=False)

async def get_db():
    async with AsyncSessionLocal() as session:
        yield session"
Trade-offs: pool_pre_ping=True prevents StaleDataError on long-idle connections. Tune pool_size based on DB max_connections / number of workers.

Keywords: websocket WebSocket real-time bidirectional push streaming accept disconnect
Description: FastAPI natively supports WebSocket connections via @router.websocket(). The endpoint accepts connections and loops receiving/sending until the client disconnects.
When to Use: When clients need server-push or bidirectional real-time communication (chat dashboards live data)
Trade-offs: WebSocket connections are long-lived — manage a connection registry for broadcasting. Use Redis pub/sub for multi-instance deployments.

Keywords: cpu bound run_in_executor ThreadPoolExecutor blocking compute async event loop offload
Description: Offload CPU-intensive synchronous work to a ThreadPoolExecutor or ProcessPoolExecutor using loop.run_in_executor to avoid blocking the async event loop.
When to Use: When a route needs CPU-heavy computation (image processing compression crypto ML inference) in an async context
Code Example:
"import asyncio
from concurrent.futures import ProcessPoolExecutor

executor = ProcessPoolExecutor()

def cpu_intensive_task(data: bytes) -> bytes:
    # runs in a separate process
    return compress(data)

@router.post('/process')
async def process(file: UploadFile):
    data = await file.read()
    loop = asyncio.get_event_loop()
    result = await loop.run_in_executor(executor, cpu_intensive_task, data)
    return Response(content=result, media_type='application/octet-stream')"
Trade-offs: ProcessPoolExecutor for true CPU parallelism (bypasses GIL). ThreadPoolExecutor for blocking I/O-bound code in sync libraries.

Keywords: StaticFiles mount path directory html serve frontend assets
Description: Mount a directory of static files (CSS JS images) using StaticFiles from Starlette. The mount happens at app level — static files are not APIRouter endpoints.
When to Use: Serving SPA frontends documentation static assets alongside your API
Code Example:
"from fastapi import FastAPI
from fastapi.staticfiles import StaticFiles

app = FastAPI()
app.mount('/static', StaticFiles(directory='static'), name='static')
# Files in ./static/ are served at /static/<filename>"
Trade-offs: Mounted static files are not part of the OpenAPI schema — they are transparent to FastAPI's routing. Use StaticFiles in production only for simple cases — use nginx/CDN in high-traffic deployments.
